item.case_name: Fact piece about a real thing
item.title: Voyager One Against the References

turns.text: Make a silent 9-second widescreen fact clip about Voyager 1, using NASA's mission page as the reference: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1/ . Three equal-length scenes: 'Launched: September 5, 1977', 'Jupiter flyby: 1979', 'Saturn flyby: 1980'. Keep 'Voyager 1' and 'Source: NASA Science' visible. Show the probe near Earth, Jupiter, then Saturn; match its real dish-and-boom design. Don't mix in Voyager 2's Uranus or Neptune visits.

item.tests: Tests whether a factual film matches a named reference in dates, mission identity, spacecraft appearance and scene order.

answer_sheet.Facts to include: Voyager 1 launched September 5, 1977, flew by Jupiter in 1979 and flew by Saturn in 1980.
answer_sheet.Length and scene order: 9 seconds total: three 3-second scenes showing Earth, Jupiter and Saturn in that order.
answer_sheet.Wording: Use exactly the five supplied labels. Keep Voyager 1 and Source: NASA Science visible throughout.
answer_sheet.Sound: Completely silent, with no narration, music or sound effects.
answer_sheet.Visual style: Your call, provided the spacecraft matches the real dish-and-boom design and the planets are recognizable.

must_haves: Three scenes appear in order, each lasting approximately three seconds: probe near Earth, near Jupiter, then near Saturn.
Each scene displays its corresponding date caption exactly, with 'Voyager 1' and 'Source: NASA Science' visible throughout.
The probe consistently has Voyager's large circular communications dish and projecting instrument booms, not solar-panel wings or a generic satellite body.
Jupiter is visibly banded and Saturn has prominent rings; neither is replaced with Uranus or Neptune.
The output contains no Uranus or Neptune flyby claims and no conflicting dates.

approvals.name: create_video_from_text

style.prompt: Create a SILENT 9-second widescreen 16:9 educational fact clip about VOYAGER 1. Exactly three scenes, each exactly 3 seconds, with hard cuts at 3.0 and 6.0 seconds. Clean scientifically grounded space visualization, restrained camera movement, readable high-contrast typography. Persistent fixed overlay at top throughout all 9 seconds, exact text: 'Voyager 1'. Persistent fixed overlay at bottom throughout all 9 seconds, exact text: 'Source: NASA Science'. Source attribution reference URL: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1/ . Use only these three dated facts and no additional claims. Scene 1, 0.0–3.0 seconds: Voyager 1 spacecraft near Earth with blue Earth in background; exact large scene caption 'Launched: September 5, 1977'. Scene 2, 3.0–6.0 seconds: same Voyager 1 spacecraft flying past Jupiter, Jupiter's banded atmosphere clearly recognizable; exact large scene caption 'Jupiter flyby: 1979'. Scene 3, 6.0–9.0 seconds: same Voyager 1 spacecraft near Saturn, Saturn's rings clearly recognizable; exact large scene caption 'Saturn flyby: 1980'. Each scene caption appears immediately at its scene start and stays stable and readable for the entire three seconds, separate from persistent title and source. Preserve a consistent accurate Voyager spacecraft design across every scene: large white parabolic high-gain dish antenna about 3.7 meters wide mounted on a compact polygonal metallic spacecraft bus, gold thermal insulation, offset long thin magnetometer boom, separate science instrument boom, three cylindrical radioisotope power units on a boom, and slender antenna rods. Recognizable asymmetric dish-and-boom deep-space probe silhouette, not a generic satellite, no solar panels, no wings, no human capsule, no large rocket body. Show the actual spacecraft, not a launch vehicle. Gentle lateral spacecraft movement, steady camera, no rapid spins, no transformations or morphing. Informative rather than suggesting all planetary visits happen simultaneously. Never show Uranus or Neptune, never mention Voyager 2, no extra planets, no invented dates, no dialogue, no narration, no music, no sound effects. End cleanly at exactly nine seconds.
